q: Which of these countries are landlocked?
fact: More than 40 countries are landlocked. Africa has the most of them - 16.

q: Which of these countries does the equator pass through?
fact: In Africa alone the equator crosses seven countries, from Sao Tome and Principe in the west to Somalia in the east.

q: Which of these rivers flow into the Black Sea?
fact: The Volga ends in the Caspian Sea, the Vistula in the Baltic, and the Rhine and Elbe in the North Sea.

q: Which of these countries share a land border with the highlighted country?
fact: Brazil borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador - ten neighbors in all, counting France through French Guiana.

q: Which of these countries border the highlighted country?
fact: Germany has nine neighbors: Denmark, Poland, the Czech Republic, Austria, Switzerland, France, Luxembourg, Belgium and the Netherlands.

q: Which of these countries share a border with the highlighted country?
fact: China and Russia share the record for the most neighbors by land: 14 countries each.

q: Which of these countries have a land border with the highlighted country?
fact: Russia's border with North Korea is less than 20 km long and runs along the Tumen River.

q: Which of these countries have a shore on the Caspian Sea?
fact: Russia is the fifth country on its shores. The Caspian is famous for its sturgeon, the fish whose eggs are sold as caviar.

q: Which of these countries have a coast on the Red Sea?
fact: Hardly any rivers flow into the Red Sea and the sun evaporates a lot of it, so it is one of the saltiest seas in the world.

q: Which of these deserts are in Asia?
fact: The Thar spans the India-Pakistan border, the Karakum covers most of Turkmenistan and the Taklamakan fills a basin in western China.

q: Which of these volcanoes are in the country whose outline is shown?
fact: Stromboli erupts so regularly, in small bursts, that sailors nicknamed it the Lighthouse of the Mediterranean.

q: Which of these islands belong to the country whose outline is shown?
fact: Greece has about 6,000 islands and islets, but only around 200 of them are inhabited. Crete is by far the largest.

q: Which of these lakes are in Africa?
fact: Lake Tanganyika is the longest freshwater lake in the world, while Lake Chad has shrunk by about 90% since the 1960s.

q: Which of these lakes are among the Great Lakes of North America?
fact: Lake Superior is the fifth. Lake Michigan is the only one of the five that lies entirely inside the United States.

q: Which of these countries does the Andes mountain range run through?
fact: The Andes run for about 7,000 km through seven countries, including Colombia, Peru and Bolivia.

q: Which of these animals are native to the highlighted country?
fact: The echidna is one of only two kinds of mammals that lay eggs. The other is the platypus, also from Australia.

q: Which of these countries have land north of the Arctic Circle?
fact: Eight countries reach above the Arctic Circle. In Iceland it only crosses the tiny island of Grimsey.

q: Which of these countries lie entirely in the Southern Hemisphere?
fact: Most of Earth's land lies north of the equator, and only about one person in ten lives south of it.

q: Which of these rivers flow through the highlighted country?
fact: The Ganges and the Brahmaputra meet in Bangladesh and build the largest river delta on Earth.

q: Which of these island countries lie in the Pacific Ocean?
fact: The Maldives, Mauritius and Seychelles are in the Indian Ocean, and Cabo Verde lies in the Atlantic off West Africa.

q: Which of these countries are home to part of the Amazon rainforest?
fact: The rainforest spreads over nine countries and territories, including French Guiana, which is part of France.

q: Which of these countries does the Tropic of Cancer cross?
fact: The Tropic of Cancer marks the farthest point north where the sun can be directly overhead, at the June solstice.

q: Which of these countries contain part of the Sahara?
fact: The Sahara stretches across about ten countries, from Mauritania on the Atlantic to Egypt and Sudan on the Red Sea.

q: Which of these mountains rise higher than 8,000 meters?
fact: All 14 mountains higher than 8,000 meters are in Asia, in the Himalayas and the Karakoram.

q: Which of these cities have served as the capital of Brazil?
fact: Salvador was the capital until 1763 and Rio de Janeiro until 1960, when the government moved to brand-new Brasília.

q: Which of these cities have served as the capital of Japan?
fact: Kyoto was the imperial capital for more than 1,000 years, from 794 until the emperor moved to Tokyo in 1869.

q: Which of these countries were once part of Yugoslavia?
fact: Yugoslavia means 'land of the South Slavs'. Montenegro was the last of these to become independent, in 2006.

q: Which of these countries were once part of the Soviet Union?
fact: The Soviet Union was made up of 15 republics. All 15 were independent countries by the end of 1991.

q: Which of these countries were once colonies of Portugal?
fact: Portuguese is still an official language in all four. East Timor became fully independent only in 2002.

q: Which of these countries became independent from France in 1960?
fact: 1960 is called the Year of Africa: 17 African countries became independent, 14 of them from France.

q: Which of these men were Roman emperors?
fact: Augustus was the first emperor. Hadrian is remembered for the wall he built across northern Britain.

q: Which of these explorers made their famous voyages for the Spanish crown?
fact: Neither of them was Spanish: Columbus came from Genoa and Magellan from Portugal.

q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World stood in the highlighted country?
fact: The lighthouse stood on the island of Pharos, a name that became the word for lighthouse in French, Italian and Spanish.

q: Which of these ancient civilizations arose in the Americas?
fact: The Olmecs of Mexico's Gulf Coast, famous for their giant stone heads, are often called the mother culture of Mesoamerica.

q: Which of these ancient sites are in the highlighted country?
fact: Chan Chan, capital of the Chimu kingdom, was the largest city built of earth in the Americas before Columbus.

q: Which of these countries founded the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951, the seed of today's EU?
fact: West Germany and the Netherlands made up the six. Sharing coal and steel bound their industries tightly together.

q: Which of these great empires arose in West Africa?
fact: The old Ghana Empire lay far north of today's Ghana, in what is now Mauritania and Mali. The modern country borrowed its name.

q: Which of these Pacific countries became independent in the 1970s?
fact: Samoa led the way in 1962 and Nauru followed in 1968, while Vanuatu had to wait until 1980.

q: Which of these are among the 'Four Great Inventions' of ancient China?
fact: Paper is the fourth. The magnetic compass was first used in China for fortune-telling, long before it guided ships.

q: In which of these countries is Spanish an official language?
fact: Spanish is official in about 20 countries. The Philippines dropped it as an official language in 1987.

q: In which of these countries is French an official language?
fact: French is widely spoken in Algeria and Morocco, but it is not an official language in either of them.

q: In which of these countries is Portuguese an official language?
fact: Equatorial Guinea added Portuguese in 2010, next to Spanish and French, to join the community of Portuguese-speaking countries.

q: Which of these languages are written in the Cyrillic alphabet?
fact: Cyrillic was created in the First Bulgarian Empire in the 800s and named in honor of Saint Cyril.

q: Which of these languages are written in the Arabic script?
fact: Turkish was written in Arabic letters too, until it switched to the Latin alphabet in 1928.

q: Which of these are Romance languages, descended from Latin?
fact: Romanian is the largest Romance language of Eastern Europe, surrounded mostly by Slavic and Hungarian speakers.

q: Which of these are Turkic languages?
fact: Turkic languages are spoken from Turkey to Siberia. Speakers of Turkish and Azerbaijani can often understand each other well.

q: Which of these festivals began in India?
fact: Diwali is the festival of lights, celebrated with oil lamps. Holi welcomes spring with clouds of colored powder.

q: Which of these writers came from Russia?
fact: Pushkin is often called the founder of modern Russian literature. Chekhov worked as a doctor while he wrote.

q: Which of these painters came from the Netherlands?
fact: Van Gogh sold very few paintings in his lifetime. Today the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam holds the largest collection of his work.

q: Which of these composers were born in Austria?
fact: Johann Strauss II, the 'Waltz King', wrote The Blue Danube. Beethoven lived in Vienna for decades but was born in Germany.

q: Which of these dances come from Latin America?
fact: Cumbia began on Colombia's Caribbean coast, blending African, Indigenous and Spanish music.

q: Which of these are official languages of South Africa?
fact: South Africa has 12 official languages. The newest, South African Sign Language, was added in 2023.

q: Which of these are Polynesian languages?
fact: Polynesian languages belong to the huge Austronesian family, which also includes Tagalog and Malay - but those two are not Polynesian.

q: Which of these are official languages of the United Nations?
fact: English and French complete the six. Arabic was the last to be added, in 1973.

q: Which of these dishes come from Italy?
fact: Risotto is made with short-grain rice from northern Italy's Po Valley, home of the biggest rice fields in Europe.

q: Which of these dishes come from the country whose outline is shown?
fact: Okonomiyaki, a savory pancake, takes its name from 'okonomi', meaning 'as you like it'.

q: Which of these dishes come from Mexico?
fact: All three are built on the corn tortilla, a staple in Mexico for thousands of years.

q: Which of these dishes come from France?
fact: Bouillabaisse is the fish stew of Marseille, and ratatouille, a vegetable stew, comes from Nice, further along the coast.

q: Which of these dishes come from India?
fact: Palak means spinach, and paneer is a fresh cheese that keeps its shape instead of melting when cooked.

q: Which of these fruits are native to the Americas?
fact: Columbus's crew first met the pineapple on Guadeloupe in 1493. In Europe it soon became a costly status symbol.

q: Which of these spices first grew only on the Maluku Islands of Indonesia, the original Spice Islands?
fact: For centuries nutmeg grew only on the tiny Banda Islands, which made it one of the most valuable goods in the world.

q: Which of these dishes come from Spain?
fact: Gazpacho is a cold tomato soup from Andalusia, made for the region's scorching summers.

q: Which of these dishes come from Peru?
fact: Lomo saltado, beef stir-fried with soy sauce, shows the influence of Chinese immigrants on Peruvian cooking.

q: Which of these dishes come from West Africa?
fact: Thieboudienne, fish with rice and vegetables, is the national dish of Senegal and is on UNESCO's heritage list.

q: Which of these are classic dishes of Korean cooking?
fact: Bulgogi means 'fire meat': thin slices of marinated beef grilled over a flame.

q: Which of these crops were staple foods of the Pacific islands long before Europeans arrived?
fact: Polynesian voyagers carried living plants of taro and breadfruit in their canoes as they settled the Pacific.

q: Which of these kinds of tea come from China?
fact: Pu-erh comes from Yunnan province and is often aged for years, sometimes decades, like a fine wine.

q: Which of these countries have a flag with only two colors?
fact: Two-color flags are common: Japan, Poland, Canada and Denmark also use just two.

q: Which of these countries have a star on their flag?
fact: The black star on Ghana's flag, raised at independence in 1957, became known as the lodestar of African freedom.

q: Which of these countries have a sun on their flag?
fact: North Macedonia's yellow sun has eight broad rays, while the suns of Uruguay and Argentina both have a human face.

q: Which of these countries have an eagle on their flag?
fact: Mexico's eagle perched on a cactus recalls the legend of how the Aztecs chose the place to build their capital.

q: Which of these countries have a flag in the same three colors as the flag shown?
fact: Many other flags share red, white and blue, among them those of Australia, Cuba, Norway and Thailand.

q: Which of these countries show the Union Jack on their national flag?
fact: Canada had the Union Jack on its flag too, until the maple leaf flag was raised for the first time in 1965.

q: Which of these countries have a flag of three vertical stripes with no emblem?
fact: Belgium's black, yellow and red come from the coat of arms of the old Duchy of Brabant.

q: Which of these countries have a crescent moon on their flag?
fact: On Uzbekistan's flag the crescent sits beside 12 stars, often said to stand for the months of the year.

q: Which of these countries have a Nordic cross on their flag?
fact: Every Nordic cross copies Denmark's flag, with the crossing set closer to the pole than to the far end.

q: Which of these countries show the Southern Cross constellation on their flag?
fact: Brazil's flag shows it too, among its 27 stars. The Southern Cross can only be seen well from the Southern Hemisphere.

q: Which of these colors appear on the flag of Jamaica?
fact: Jamaica's flag is often said to be the only national flag with no red, white or blue in it.

q: Which of these colors appear on the flag of Brazil?
fact: The white band across the blue globe carries the motto 'Ordem e Progresso' - Order and Progress.

q: Which of these capital cities stand on the Danube?
fact: No other river in the world flows through as many national capitals as the Danube - four of them.

q: Which of these cities are national capitals?
fact: Canberra and Brasília were both planned and built from scratch in the 1900s to serve as capitals.

q: Which of these landmarks are in Paris?
fact: The Louvre was a royal palace for centuries before it opened as a museum in 1793. It is home to the Mona Lisa.

q: Which of these landmarks are in China?
fact: The Forbidden City in Beijing was home to China's emperors for almost 500 years, until 1912.

q: Which of these cities are state capitals in Australia?
fact: Sydney and Melbourne are the other two state capitals. Darwin and Canberra are capitals of territories, not states.

q: Which of these cities are in Canada?
fact: Calgary hosts the Stampede every July, a giant rodeo and festival that draws over a million visitors.

q: Which of these cities lie on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea?
fact: Lisbon and Casablanca face the Atlantic instead, and Cairo lies well over 100 km inland on the Nile.

q: Which of these cities stand on the Nile?
fact: Juba, the capital of South Sudan, lies on the White Nile. Aswan is home to the High Dam, which created Lake Nasser.

q: Which of these landmarks are in the United States?
fact: Each of the four presidents' faces carved into Mount Rushmore is about 18 meters tall.

q: Which of these capital cities are in Africa?
fact: Windhoek, the capital of Namibia, sits on a high plateau about 1,650 meters above sea level.

q: Which of these landmarks stand in Rome?
fact: The Pantheon's dome, nearly 1,900 years old, is still the largest dome of unreinforced concrete in the world.

q: Which of these cities are in India?
fact: Bengaluru is the center of India's tech industry and is often called the Silicon Valley of India.

q: Which of these cities are in the highlighted country?
fact: Dunedin takes its name from Dun Eideann, the old Gaelic name of Edinburgh, a nod to its Scottish founders.

q: In which of these countries do cars drive on the left?
fact: About a third of the world's people live in countries that drive on the left, many of them former British colonies.

q: Which of these countries have more than 100 million people?
fact: Only about 15 countries have passed 100 million people. Germany, the most populous in the EU, has around 84 million.

q: In which of these countries do the Maasai people live?
fact: The Maasai are known for their red shuka cloth and the adumu, a dance in which young men leap high into the air.

q: In which of these countries do the Sami people traditionally live?
fact: Norway has the largest Sami population, and has had an elected Sami Parliament since 1989.

q: Which of these countries have fewer than one million people?
fact: Iceland has only about 400,000 people, and about two-thirds of them live in and around Reykjavik.

q: In which of these countries are most people Buddhist?
fact: The Buddha was born in what is now Nepal, yet most people in Nepal today are Hindu.

q: Which of these countries have more than a billion people?
fact: India overtook China as the most populous country in 2023. Each has around 1.4 billion people.

q: Which of these countries have a king or emperor as head of state?
fact: Sweden's king has a purely ceremonial role, like most monarchs in Europe today.

q: Which of these countries have won the men's FIFA World Cup?
fact: Spain won its second title in 2026. The Netherlands has reached three finals, in 1974, 1978 and 2010, without ever winning one.

q: Which of these countries have hosted the Summer Olympic Games?
fact: Mexico City in 1968 hosted the first Summer Games in Latin America. Seoul followed in 1988.

q: Which of these countries have hosted the Winter Olympic Games?
fact: St. Moritz in Switzerland hosted twice, in 1928 and 1948. Snowy Sweden and Finland have never hosted the Winter Games.

q: Which of these sports were invented in the United States?
fact: Volleyball was invented in Holyoke, Massachusetts, in 1895 - just four years after basketball, in a nearby town.

q: Which of these countries have won the men's Rugby World Cup?
fact: England is the only team from the Northern Hemisphere to have won it, in 2003. France has lost three finals.

q: Which of these cities host one of tennis's four Grand Slam tournaments?
fact: Paris is played on red clay and London's Wimbledon on grass, while Melbourne and New York use hard courts.

q: Which of these martial arts come from Japan?
fact: Kendo, 'the way of the sword', is fought with bamboo swords and protective armor.

q: Which of these countries have hosted matches of the men's FIFA World Cup?
fact: Canada hosted World Cup matches for the first time in 2026, together with the United States and Mexico.

q: Which of these cities have hosted the Summer Olympic Games more than once?
fact: London (1908, 1948, 2012) and Paris (1900, 1924, 2024) have hosted three times each. Los Angeles will join them in 2028.

q: Which of these countries are Full Members of the International Cricket Council, allowed to play Test matches?
fact: There are 12 Full Members. Ireland and Afghanistan were the latest to join, both in 2017.

q: Which of these countries use the euro?
fact: Croatia swapped its kuna for the euro in 2023, and Bulgaria became the 21st member in 2026.

q: Which of these companies were founded in Japan?
fact: Nintendo was founded in Kyoto in 1889 - as a maker of playing cards.

q: Which of these car brands come from Germany?
fact: Volkswagen simply means 'people's car' in German.

q: Which of these currencies are used in Africa?
fact: The rand is named after the Witwatersrand, the ridge near Johannesburg where gold was discovered in 1886.

q: Which of these countries call their currency the peso?
fact: The peso goes back to the Spanish silver dollar, a coin traded around the whole world from the 1500s on.

q: Which of these countries use the US dollar as their official currency?
fact: Ecuador switched to the US dollar in 2000 and El Salvador in 2001.

q: Which of these currencies are used in Asia?
fact: The Japanese yen, the Chinese yuan and the Korean won all take their names from the same old word for a round coin.

q: Which of these companies were founded in Sweden?
fact: IKEA's name joins the initials of its founder, Ingvar Kamprad, with those of his family farm, Elmtaryd, and his village, Agunnaryd.

q: Which of these Pacific countries use the Australian dollar as their currency?
fact: Kiribati and Tuvalu also mint their own coins, which are used alongside Australian banknotes.

q: Which of these countries are larger than India by area?
fact: India is the seventh-largest country in the world. Argentina, in eighth place, is the next one down.

q: Which of these countries cover less than 100 square km?
fact: Liechtenstein covers about 160 square km, and Malta and the Maldives are each around 300.

q: Which of these island countries share a land border with another country?
fact: Indonesia shares three islands: New Guinea with Papua New Guinea, Timor with East Timor and Borneo with Malaysia and Brunei.

q: Which of these capital cities lie more than 2,000 meters above sea level?
fact: La Paz, the seat of Bolivia's government, is higher still, at about 3,600 meters.

q: Which of these countries are made up of more than 100 islands?
fact: Nauru is a single island, while Solomon Islands is spread over roughly 900.

q: In which of these countries is the capital NOT the largest city?
fact: Nigeria moved its capital from Lagos to Abuja, a new city near the center of the country, in 1991.

q: Which of these rivers are longer than 6,000 km?
fact: The Nile and the Amazon both run for about 6,400 to 6,650 km. Which one is longer depends on how they are measured.
